vignette: He stands at his worktable, fingers tracing the edge of a bolt of navy wool when the morning radio crackles. The anchor's voice drops to a serious register, and his shoulders hike instantly. His breath hitches. Three years ago, a similar broadcast interrupted a Tuesday at the Al-Masra market. He was measuring a client's inseam when the world split open. The first shockwave threw him backward into a rack of silk. Glass rained down. Then came a second, heavier impact, followed by a silence so complete he heard his own heartbeat hammering against his ribs. He lay there, listening to moans and distant sirens, waiting for the ground to shake again. When he finally stood, his hands were raw, his lungs filled with dust and copper. He walked home through streets where familiar faces were unrecognizable, past his shop's torn awning. Now, at thirty-three, he runs a modest tailoring workshop above a grocery store. He is single, lives quietly, and has not left his neighborhood in nearly two years. His work demands exactness. A quarter-inch deviation ruins a jacket, and his clients expect perfection. Yet his hands, once steady enough to run a needle through canvas, tremble when he picks up his shears. The sewing machine's motor has become a trigger. When the hum reaches a certain pitch, his vision narrows. He sees smoke again. He drops the thread. He turns off the machine, steps to the stairwell, and watches the street for anyone who looks like they might run. He tells himself he is checking for fire escapes, but he knows he is counting bodies. Sleep offers little refuge. He wakes at 3:14 a.m., convinced the floorboards are vibrating. His sheets tangle around his ankles. He lies still until his breathing steadies. He drafts patterns with meticulous care, but his mind drifts to exits, load-bearing walls, the ceiling above his bed. He has stopped accepting rush orders. The pressure to meet deadlines feels indistinguishable from a countdown he imagines in crowded places. His clients notice his distance. They speak, and he replies with precise measurements, but his gaze stays past their left shoulder. He eats at the same counter, sits with his back to the wall, scans the room before the first customer arrives. He prefers dark, heavy cottons. They remind him of uniforms dragged across the asphalt that afternoon, but they also hide him. He presses his palms flat against the cutting table when memories surface uninvited. Singed thread makes him step back. Rain makes him close his eyes and count to ten. He does not cry. He measures, cuts, and stitches in quiet repetitions, as if maintaining the rhythm might keep the chaos at bay. In the present session, he sits on the edge of the chair, legs apart, boots planted on the floor. He speaks in a measured tone, describing how he reorganized his shop to eliminate corners, how he arrives an hour early to scan the block, how he keeps a metal ruler in his pocket to weigh down his coat. When the traffic light outside changes, he flinches. When the therapist leans forward, he adjusts his posture. He explains that he no longer dreams of the explosion. Instead, he dreams of standing in a room where everyone sleeps, while he watches the door. He finishes, folds his hands over his knees, and waits. The room is quiet. His breathing is slow, deliberate. He is still here.
